source.title: Do Large Language Models Mirror Cognitive Language Processing?
source.authors: Yuqi Ren; Renren Jin; Tongxuan Zhang; Deyi Xiong

record.tranche_reason: The study measures representational similarity between LLMs and human fMRI signals, not similarity between independently trained models. Its results therefore concern a related construct and do not test any claim version.
record.gate_note: The RSA results, scaling comparisons, prompt comparisons, sentiment comparison, and model-evaluation correlations are about LLM–brain similarity. They do not measure convergence between models, cross-modal image–caption alignment, shared features, or interchangeability between models.
record.test_reason: The study measures RSA similarity between LLM sentence embeddings and human fMRI signals. It never compares representations between independently trained models, seeds or modalities. LLM–brain similarity is a related but different construct, so it tests no version. It is recorded under fits_no_version. The paper does not cite either original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that more pre-training data, larger models and alignment training increase LLM–brain similarity. Explicit prompts help, and noisy prompts may attenuate it. They add three further points the paraphrase omits: alignment training increases sensitivity to prompts, LLMs resemble humans more for positive sentiment, and the trends hold across RSA metrics and the intermediate layer. They propose LLM–brain similarity as a new LLM evaluation signal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses RSA to compare LLM representations with fMRI representations of human brain activity; it does not compare representations between independently trained models.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported LLM–brain similarity varies with training stage, prompt strategy, sentiment polarity, and representation layer. The study reports that trends across the four RSA metrics are roughly consistent.

fits_no_version.finding: LLM–brain RSA similarity rises with model size within families. For example, LLaMA2 rises from 0.2207 (7B) to 0.2568 (70B), Pearson, final layer. The same trend holds at the intermediate layer (Table 3) and under all three prompt conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger LLMs' text representations align more with human fMRI language representations. This bears on PRH's brain-alignment argument, not on model–model convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: Alignment-trained (SFT/RLHF/DPO) variants show higher LLM–brain similarity than their base models. For example, LLaMA3-70B rises from 0.2778 to 0.2938 (instruct), final layer, Pearson.
Across the 10 Amber checkpoints, LLM–brain similarity gradually improves with more pre-training data. Values appear only in a figure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM–brain representational similarity can increase with pre-training data size.

fits_no_version.finding: Explicit prompts generally raise LLM–brain similarity over no prompt; noisy prompts slightly lower it. Table 4 gives explicit-minus-none deltas of 0.0014 to 0.0351, largest for aligned 70B models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt formulation affects measured LLM–brain similarity.

fits_no_version.finding: LLM–brain similarity is reported significantly higher for positive than for negative sentiment concepts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM–brain similarity differs across sentiment polarities.

fits_no_version.finding: LLM–brain similarity correlates positively with MMLU, HellaSwag, Chatbot Arena Elo and AlpacaEval (Figure 5). LLaMA3-70B-instruct is an outlier on the alignment evaluations.

record.problems: The fMRI stimulus texts are exclusively English. The authors used 5 subjects who participated in all three experiments and randomly selected 1,000 voxels per subject. Some results are presented only in figures without numerical values in the text. The study cannot assess closed-source LLMs, as acknowledged by the authors.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 and Table 3 also report Euclidean, Cosine, and Spearman results for each model; these metric-specific entries were not extracted. Figure 3 has separate plotted results for individual LLMs, and Figure 4 has plotted model-by-polarity results; only the authors’ aggregate descriptions are recorded. Figure 5’s benchmark correlation plots are summarized in fits_no_version rather than entered as rows because they do not measure the claim’s representational convergence.

untested.parts: No model-to-model alignment is measured. Scaling is related only to LLM–brain similarity.
No vision models and no image–caption pairs.
No comparison across seeds or of shared features.
No mapping, stitching or interchangeability test between models.
No interpretable features or circuits compared across models.
Metric and layer variation is reported only for LLM–brain RSA, not inter-model convergence.
No test of plateauing or shared-data causes of inter-model alignment.

record.verdict_notes: The relation is set to 'discusses' only as the closest available option; the paper neither cites nor discusses the Platonic hypothesis. Its scaling result resembles PRH's brain-alignment argument but concerns brain alignment, not model–model convergence, so no row is linked to a version. Table 4 prompt deltas are not extracted as rows; this is not needed for any version. The text contains an error: it says Mistral-7B scores 0.2573 when comparing it with M-alpha. Table 2 gives Mistral-7B 0.2533 and M-beta 0.2573, so M-alpha (0.2481) is still lower. Only 5 fMRI subjects and 1,000 random voxels per subject are used, and the stimuli are English only.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of representations between independently trained models.
No paired vision and language models or image–caption representations.
No comparison across random seeds or shared features/subspaces between networks.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test between models.
No recurring interpretable features or circuits are assessed.
The study compares RSA metrics for LLM–brain similarity, not measures or input choices for inter-model convergence.
No test of whether inter-model alignment plateaus or is caused by shared training data or objectives.

rows.subject: Amber checkpoints (10 selected checkpoints)
rows.operation_detail: Measured LLM–brain similarity across checkpoints trained on increasing amounts of pre-training data
rows.value: Figure 2 shows gradual improvement as pre-training data size increases; individual values not stated
rows.note: A data-size trend for LLM–brain similarity, not inter-model convergence.

rows.subject: 23 LLMs (aggregate description)
rows.operation_detail: Compared LLM–brain similarity under prompt-appending strategies
rows.value: Figure 3 shows explicit prompts generally outperforming the other two strategies; numeric values not stated
rows.note: The authors state noisy prompts may attenuate alignment; no inter-model comparison is made.

rows.subject: 23 LLMs (aggregate description)

rows.value: Figure 3 shows no-prompt tends to outperform noisy prompts for most LLMs; numeric values not stated
rows.note: The paper also says scaling and LLM–brain similarity remain positively correlated across the three prompt conditions.
